{{Short description|Mathematical concept}}
{{about|the notion in several complex variables|the notion in convex analysis|pseudoconvex function}}
In [[mathematics]], more precisely in the theory of functions of [[Function of several complex variables|several complex variables]], a '''pseudoconvex set''' is a special type of [[open set]] in the ''n''-dimensional complex space '''C'''<sup>''n''</sup>. Pseudoconvex sets are important, as they allow for classification of [[domain of holomorphy|domains of holomorphy]]. 

Let <math>G\subset {\mathbb{C}}^n</math> be a [[Domain (mathematical analysis)|domain]]. One says that <math>G</math> is ''pseudoconvex'' (or ''[[Friedrich Hartogs|Hartogs]] pseudoconvex'') if there exists a [[continuous function|continuous]] [[plurisubharmonic function]] <math>\varphi</math> on <math>G</math> such that the set <math>\{ z \in G \mid \varphi(z) < x \}</math> is a [[relatively compact]] subset of <math>G</math> for all  [[real number]]s <math>x.</math> In other words, a domain is pseudoconvex if <math>G</math> has a continuous plurisubharmonic [[bounded exhaustion function|exhaustion function]]. Every (geometrically) [[convex set]] is pseudoconvex. However, there are pseudoconvex domains which are not geometrically convex.

When <math>G</math> has a <math>C^2</math> (twice [[smooth function|continuously differentiable]]) [[boundary (topology)|boundary]], this notion is the same as Levi pseudoconvexity, which is easier to work with. More specifically, with a  <math>C^2</math> boundary, it can be shown that  <math>G</math> has a defining function, i.e., that there exists  <math>\rho: \mathbb{C}^n \to  \mathbb{R} </math> which is  <math>C^2</math> so that  <math>G=\{\rho <0 \}</math>, and <math>\partial G =\{\rho =0\}</math>.  Now,  <math>G</math> is pseudoconvex if and only if for every  <math>p \in \partial G</math> and <math>w</math> in the complex tangent space at p, that is,  

:<math> \nabla \rho(p) w = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{\partial \rho (p)}{ \partial z_j }w_j =0 </math>, we have
:<math>\sum_{i,j=1}^n \frac{\partial^2 \rho(p)}{\partial z_i \partial \bar{z_j} } w_i \bar{w_j} \geq 0.</math>

The definition above is analogous to definitions of convexity in Real Analysis.

If <math>G</math> does not have a <math>C^2</math> boundary, the following approximation result can be useful. 

'''Proposition 1'''   ''If  <math>G</math> is pseudoconvex, then there exist [[bounded set|bounded]], strongly Levi pseudoconvex domains  <math>G_k \subset G</math> with <math>C^\infty</math> ([[smooth function|smooth]]) boundary which are relatively compact in <math>G</math>, such that''  

:<math>G = \bigcup_{k=1}^\infty G_k.</math>

This is because once we have a <math>\varphi</math> as in the definition we can actually find a ''C''<sup>∞</sup> exhaustion function.

==The case ''n'' = 1==
In one complex dimension, every open domain is pseudoconvex.
